facts.statement: The genus Thalassodromeus was described by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos in 2002.
facts.quote: authority: Kellner & Campos, 2002

facts.statement: The original skull of Thalassodromeus was discovered in 1983 in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: The original skull, discovered in 1983 in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil, was collected in several pieces.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus possessed one of the largest known pterosaur skulls, measuring around 1.42 meters in length, and one of the largest cranial crests of any vertebrate.
facts.quote: Thalassodromeus had one of the largest known skulls among pterosaurs, around 1.42 m long, with one of the proportionally largest cranial crests of any vertebrate.

facts.statement: Although only the skull is known, Thalassodromeus is estimated to have had a wingspan between 4.2 and 4.5 meters.
facts.quote: Though only the skull is known, the animal is estimated to have had a wingspan of 4.2 to 4.5 m.

facts.statement: The crest of Thalassodromeus was lightly built, extending from the tip of the upper jaw to the back of the skull with a unique V-shaped notch at the end.
facts.quote: The crest was lightly built and ran from the tip of the upper jaw to beyond the back of the skull, ending in a unique V-shaped notch.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had toothless jaws with sharp upper and lower edges.
facts.quote: The jaws were toothless, and had sharp upper and lower edges.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus had large nasoantorbital fenestrae combining the antorbital opening and bony nostril, and a concave palate.
facts.quote: Its skull had large nasoantorbital fenestrae (opening that combined the antorbital fenestra in front of the eye with the bony nostril), and part of its palate was concave.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the crest of Thalassodromeus served functions like thermoregulation and display, though it likely had multiple functions.
facts.quote: Several theories have been suggested to explain the function of Thalassodromeuss crest, including thermoregulation and display, but it likely had more than one function.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, where it coexisted with other pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and animals.
facts.quote: Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, where it coexisted with many other types of pterosaurs, dinosaurs and other animals.

facts.statement: The first known specimen of Thalassodromeus was collected in 1983 near Santana do Cariri in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: The first known specimen of this pterosaur (an extinct order of flying reptiles) was collected in 1983 near the town of Santana do Cariri in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: The skull was first reported in a 1984 Italian book and preliminarily described in 1990 by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
facts.quote: The skull was first reported in a 1984 Italian book, and preliminarily described and figured in 1990 by palaeontologists Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.

facts.statement: In 2002, Kellner and Campos formally described and named the species Thalassodromeus sethi, using skull DGM 1476-R as the holotype.
facts.quote: In 2002, Kellner and Campos described and named the new genus and species Thalassodromeus sethi, skull DGM 1476-R being the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: In 2006, David M. Martill and Darren Naish suggested that Thalassodromeus was a junior synonym of Tupuxuara, a theory later rejected by Kellner and Campos.
facts.quote: In 2006, palaeontologists David M. Martill and Darren Naish suggested that Thalassodromeus was a junior synonym of the related genus Tupuxuara, which was named by Kellner and Campos in 1988 based on fossils from the same formation.

facts.statement: In 2015, Jaime A. Headden and Herbert B. N. Campos described the jaw tip of Thalassodromeus as a new genus, Banguela oberlii, interpreting it as a toothless dsungaripterid.
facts.quote: Palaeontologists Jaime A. Headden and Herbert B. N. Campos coined the new binomial Banguela oberlii, based on their reinterpretation of the jaw tip as belonging to a toothless member of the family Dsungaripteridae, in 2015.

facts.statement: In 2018, Rubi V. Pêgas, Fabiana R. Costa, and Kellner re-described the holotype and assigned the jaw tip back to Thalassodromeus as the distinct species T. oberlii.
facts.quote: In their 2018 re-description of the further-prepared T. sethi holotype skull, palaeontologists Rubi V. Pêgas, Fabiana R. Costa, and Kellner assigned B. oberlii back to Thalassodromeus while recognising it as a distinct species, and thereby created the new combination T. oberlii.

facts.statement: In 2020, James McPhee and colleagues argued that Banguela was a valid genus belonging to the family Chaoyangopteridae rather than a dsungaripterid.
facts.quote: In 2020, palaeontlogist James McPhee and colleagues considered Banguela a valid genus, and instead classified it as a member of the family Chaoyangopteridae, and did not find a dsungaripterid identity well-supported.

facts.statement: In 2015, Gerald Grellet Tinner and Vlad A. Codrea named T. sebesensis based on a crest fragment found near the Sebeș River in Romania.
facts.quote: In 2015 palaeontologists Gerald Grellet Tinner and Vlad A. Codrea named a new species, T. sebesensis, based on what they interpreted as part of a cranial crest in a concretion found near the Sebeș River in Romania.

facts.statement: Gareth J. Dyke and colleagues rejected the identification of T. sebesensis as a pterosaur, arguing instead that the fossil was a misidentified part of the turtle Kallokibotion bajazidi.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Gareth J. Dyke and a large team of colleagues immediately rejected the pterosaurian identification of the T. sebesensis fossil, instead arguing that it was a misidentified part of a plastron (lower shell) of the prehistoric turtle Kallokibotion bajazidi (named in 1923).

facts.statement: The skull of Thalassodromeus sethi was estimated to be 1.42 meters long.
facts.quote: The entire skull is estimated to have been 1.42 m long

facts.statement: Based on related pterosaurs, the wingspan of Thalassodromeus was estimated to be between 4.2 and 4.5 meters.
facts.quote: Based on related pterosaurs, its wingspan was 4.2 to 4.5 m

facts.statement: The hindlimbs of Thalassodromeus were eighty percent the length of the forelimbs, a unique ratio among pterodactyloids.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs were eighty percent that of the forelimb length, a unique ratio among pterodactyloids

facts.statement: The crest of Thalassodromeus varied in thickness from 1 to 10.5 millimeters.
facts.quote: The crest varied from 1 to 10.5 mm in thickness

facts.statement: A small 46-millimeter opening was present above the eye socket, piercing the base of the crest.
facts.quote: A small, 46 mm opening was present above the orbit (eye socket), piercing the basal part of the crest

facts.statement: Like all members of its clade, Thalassodromeus had toothless jaws.
facts.quote: As in all members of its clade, the jaws were edentulous (toothless).

facts.statement: The snout of Thalassodromeus was 650 millimeters long from the tip of the premaxilla to the jaw joint.
facts.quote: The rostrum (snout) was 650 mm long from the tip of the premaxilla to the joint where the quadrate bone of the skull connected with the articular bone of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Although incomplete, the total length of the lower jaw of Thalassodromeus sethi is estimated at 670 millimeters.
facts.quote: Although the lower jaw of T. sethi is incomplete, its total length is estimated at 670 mm

facts.statement: The mandibular symphysis occupied 47 percent of the lower jaw's total length.
facts.quote: 47 percent of which was occupied by the mandibular symphysis.

facts.statement: The symphyseal shelf extended for 170 millimeters and had a flat surface.
facts.quote: The symphyseal shelf, the upper surface of the symphysis, extended for 170 mm and had a flat surface.

facts.statement: The possible species Thalassodromeus oberlii differed from T. sethi by having an upper mandibular symphysis surface slightly shorter than the lower surface.
facts.quote: The possible species T. oberlii differed from T. sethi and other relatives by the upper surface of its mandibular symphysis being slightly shorter than the lower surface

facts.statement: Researchers Kellner and Campos originally classified Thalassodromeus in the family Tapejaridae due to its large crest and large nasoantorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos originally assigned Thalassodromeus to the family Tapejaridae, based on its large crest and large nasoantorbital fenestra.

facts.statement: In 2006, Martill and Naish argued that Tapejaridae was an unnatural group and placed Thalassodromeus as a sister taxon to the family Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: Martill and Naish considered Tapejaridae a paraphyletic (unnatural) group in 2006, and found Tupuxuara (which included Thalassodromeus in their analysis) to be the sister taxon to the family Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: In 2007, Kellner and Campos defended the family Tapejaridae by splitting it into Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae, the latter containing Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos defended the validity of Tapejaridae in 2007, dividing it into two clades: Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae, the latter containing Thalassodromeus (the type genus) and Tupuxuara.

facts.statement: Mark Witton elevated Thalassodrominae to the family level Thalassodromidae and placed it within Neoazhdarchia.
facts.quote: Witton further converted the subfamily name Thalassodrominae into the family name Thalassodromidae, and considered the clade part of Neoazhdarchia.

facts.statement: A 2011 study by Pinheiro and colleagues supported grouping Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae within the family Tapejaridae alongside Chaoyangopterinae.
facts.quote: A 2011 analysis by Pinheiro and colleagues upheld the grouping of the clades Tapejarinae and Thalassodrominae in the family Tapejaridae, joined by the Chaoyangopterinae.

facts.statement: In 2021, Gabriela M. Cerqueira and colleagues identified the genus Kariridraco as the sister taxon to Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.
facts.quote: In 2021, palaeontologist Gabriela M. Cerqueira and colleagues found their new genus Kariridraco to be the sister taxon of Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara.

facts.statement: In 2023, Rubi Pêgas and colleagues argued that despite classification disagreements, the species within the Thalassodromeus clade have remained consistent, favoring the name Thalassodromidae.
facts.quote: In 2023, having considered that the clade containing Thalassodromeus and Tupuxuara has received two different denominations throughout the years (Thalassodromidae and Thalassodrominae), palaeontologist Rubi Pêgas and colleagues argued that despite the disagreements between the position of said clade within Azhdarchoidea, the species contained within it have almost always been consistent.

facts.statement: The classification of Thalassodromeus and its relatives remains one of the most contentious issues in pterosaur research.
facts.quote: The classification of Thalassodromeus and its closest relatives is one of the most contentious issues regarding their group.

facts.statement: Martill and Naish suggested the crest developed late in life and was likely related to sexual display, with maturity assessable by crest size.
facts.quote: This suggests that the development of the crest happened late in the growth of an individual, was probably related to sexual display, and the sexual maturity of a given specimen could be assessed by the size and disposition of the crest.

facts.statement: Witton agreed in 2013 that the large crests of adult thalassodromids were more important for behavior than for physiology.
facts.quote: In 2013, Witton agreed that the substantially larger crests of adult thalassodromids indicated that they were more important for behavioural activities than for physiology.

facts.statement: Witton concluded the crest's blood vessels were likely for nutrient transport like bird beaks, not primarily for thermoregulation.
facts.quote: He concluded that the crest's blood-vessel patterns did not differ much from those seen on bones under the beaks of birds, which are used for transporting nutrients to the bone and soft tissues rather than for thermoregulation.

facts.statement: Pêgas and colleagues suggested the T. sethi holotype's crest shape may correlate with one sex and result from sexual selection.
facts.quote: Pêgas and colleagues noted that sexual dimorphism in crest size and shape has been proposed for some pterosaurs; the crest shape seen in the T. sethi holotype may correlate with one sex and may have been the result of sexual selection.

facts.statement: The concave palatine bones of Thalassodromeus were hypothesized to help the animal momentarily store food while skimming.
facts.quote: Unlike skimmers and other pterosaurs, the palatine bones of Thalassodromeus were concave, which the writers suggested could have helped it momentarily store food.

facts.statement: In 2007, biophysicist Stuart Humphries and colleagues debated the skimming feeding hypothesis, arguing it was based on anatomy rather than biomechanical data.
facts.quote: In 2007, biophysicist Stuart Humphries and colleagues questioned whether any pterosaurs would have commonly fed by skimming and said that such conclusions had been based on anatomical comparisons rather than biomechanical data.

facts.statement: In 2013, Witton argued that pterosaurs likely did not skim-feed because they lacked virtually all anatomical adaptations for this behavior.
facts.quote: Witton said in 2013 that although skim-feeding had been suggested for many pterosaur groups, the idea was criticised in recent years; pterosaurs lacked virtually all adaptations for skim-feeding, making it unlikely that they fed this way.

facts.statement: A 2015 study by Pêgas and Kellner indicated that Thalassodromeus sethi had a strong bite force based on its well-developed jaw muscles.
facts.quote: Pêgas and Kellner presented a reconstruction of the mandibular muscles of T. sethi at a conference in 2015. They found that its well-developed jaw muscles differed from those of the possible dip-feeder Anhanguera and the terrestrially stalking azhdarchids, indicating that T. sethi had a strong bite force.

facts.statement: Williams hypothesized that the crest was inflatable with blood to act like a fan, helping change head attitude during flight and water contact without requiring powerful neck muscles.
facts.quote: Williams speculated that the crest would be inflatable with blood and presented varying air resistance, which he compared to a handheld fan; this would have helped the animal change the attitude of the head during flight (and during contact with water), keeping it from rotating without powerful neck muscles.

facts.statement: Kellner and Campos rejected the inflatable crest hypothesis, noting that compressed bones would not allow it and that the sperm whale analogy was unconvincing for flying animals.
facts.quote: Kellner and Campos rejected the idea of an inflatable crest, since its compressed bones would not allow this; they did not find the sperm-whale analogy convincing in relation to flying animals, noting that spermaceti is more likely to be used during aggression or for sonar.

facts.statement: Witton suggested that thalassodromids had terrestrial abilities comparable to azhdarchids due to similar limb proportions.
facts.quote: Witton suggested that the proportional similarity between the limbs of thalassodromids and azhdarchids also indicates that their terrestrial abilities would have been comparable.

facts.statement: Thalassodromids likely had limbs capable of long strides, with short, compact feet making these mechanics efficient.
facts.quote: Their limbs would have been capable of long strides, and their short, compact feet would have made these mechanics efficient.

facts.statement: Witton cautioned that more analysis was needed to confirm the terrestrial abilities of thalassodromids.
facts.quote: Witton cautioned that more analysis of thalassodromids was needed to determine this.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus lived approximately 110 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, which dates to the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period (about 110million years ago).

facts.statement: The environment where Thalassodromeus lived had a tropical climate similar to modern-day Brazil.
facts.quote: The formation's tropical climate largely corresponded to today's Brazilian climate.

facts.statement: Thalassodromeus lived approximately between 122 and 109 million years ago.

facts.statement: A lower jaw fragment attributed to Thalassodromeus suggests an individual with a wingspan of 5.3 meters.

facts.statement: The function of Thalassodromeus's crest is unknown, though it may have been used for sexual display, species recognition, or thermoregulation.

facts.statement: Kellner hypothesized that Thalassodromeus fed by dragging its lower jaw in the water while flying, similar to a skimmer.
facts.quote: Kellner creyó que Thalassodromeus se alimentaba de forma muy similar al actual rayador; arrastrando su mandíbula inferior en el agua mientras volaba.

facts.statement: Later research suggested that Thalassodromeus's jaw and neck anatomy made skimming water while flying energetically unfeasible.

facts.statement: While Kellner classified Thalassodromeus in the family Tapejaridae, other analyses place it in the group Thalassodrominae, closer to the family Azhdarchidae.
